magen-avraham/1:ד: And examine [this] in a place where smell applies. For example, when the oven is small and closed and the forbidden and permitted items are exposed inside the oven, as written in Yoreh De'ah siman 108 and in Shach there; and Rama wrote that in a place of loss one may be lenient, and it appears to me only when it is slightly open in a place where the smoke exits; for when completely closed, even with other prohibitions Rama wrote one may not be lenient except in a place of loss, and therefore with chametz, even in a place of loss, it is forbidden. And furthermore, for Tosafot on Avodah Zarah are stringent even in a large open oven — see there; and also the view of Rif, chapter 6 of Chullin, to forbid, for he wrote that Rav said smell is meaningless according to him, because he holds min b'mino b'mashahu, and we hold in this siman it implies that Pesach, which is b'mashahu — for everyone it is meaningful; and also Ran wrote that smell in any amount is meaningful, and with this we reject the proof of Maharil in his responsum — see there; and if so, we have no authority to permit, for in Mordechai no explanation is found to permit except to prove from what Mordechai wrote that we hold smell is not meaningful — from this we learn that he holds chametz equals other prohibitions in this; and furthermore, in Choshen Mishpat siman 25 Sma wrote that everywhere we rule like Rif except in a place where Tosafot disagree, and here both of them equally forbid; therefore at minimum one may not be lenient when completely closed and small, even in a place of loss, and it is enough for us to be lenient when slightly open, for who will come after Rama's ruling. And all this is in roasting; but in cooking, since with other prohibitions it is permitted l'chatchila to cook in one oven, if so from this we learn there is no smell at all, if so with chametz at minimum b'dieved it is permitted; and even though Rama wrote that if the oven is closed, even in cooking it is forbidden even b'dieved — behold, he himself wrote in Darkei Moshe that in the Gemara and in all the poskim there is to permit in cooking, only that since Orchot Chaim and Mahariv were stringent about hot food insulated for Shabbat one may not be lenient — end of his words; and it appears Orchot Chaim of Rama was not as we said before us, and one must say hot food is considered like roasting, and regarding baking, in cooking we hold it is permitted — end of his words; and the truth is with him, for Rashba wrote the reason that cooking does not forbid is because it has no smell, and our eyes see that hot food insulated for Shabbat has a strong smell, and therefore Mahariv holds it forbids; and this is his language in Yesh S..., page 5: and if the oven is closed and the pot is not well covered, that it has a hole through which it can absorb from it to the outside — forbidden, for a covered pot that has no place for the smell to exit — it is known that insulation causes absorption and it is forbidden even in cooking — end of his words; but if they cook on a weekday for an hour or two and close the oven for that period, one need not be stringent except regarding insulation for Shabbat, and it is possible that Rama also intended this; and even though Beit Yosef in siman 97 disagrees with Rashba and brings proof from the Gemara that the reason is because the pot interrupts, therefore Shulchan Aruch did not conclude what Rashba wrote that the smell of what is cooking does not forbid as much; and if so, even in insulation or pot roasting in an oven one should be lenient; nevertheless it appears to me that Rashba's words are correct, for even though the smell does not exit from the sides, nevertheless it exits from above, and behold the proof regarding peshtida — we require that there not be a hole on top; and that which the Gemara answers, like two pots — Rashi explained: a skewer from here and a skewer from here and a large mound of coals or dirt in the middle — end of his words; it implies only regarding a large mound through which smell cannot rise above it, but the interruption of a pot does not count; and that which he answered initially with two pots — the one who asked understood it deals with cooking, and cooking has no smell, therefore he questioned seif 4 — see there; and if so, the law of hot food insulated [for Shabbat] is like roasting, and all the more so pot roasting as is done on Yom Tov; but when one cooked in an oven for an hour, even if one closed the oven one need not be stringent; and he wrote in Yesh S...: and a somewhat large oven, even though it does not hold twelve se'ah, is permitted b'dieved; and if it has a hole from the side besides the opening, it is permitted even l'chatchila since the hole is in a high place and the oven is high, but it is difficult to permit before the masses — end of his words; and it is possible that one may rely on this for chametz on Pesach in a place of loss to permit if the oven is high and the hole open in a high place: what he wrote above that with chametz we do not find [an issur of] davar charif — not precise, for in Arshak it is called sharp as Taz wrote in Yoreh De'ah.
magen-avraham/3:ג: If it reached yad soledes bo. One might say that in siman 467 seif 12 he concludes to forbid even cold, and one must say that there it deals with water that is moist and imparts taste; but here it deals with a case where they removed the chicken from the pot near evening and placed it in a bowl without gravy, and when Pesach entered it was still boiling — then it is not forbidden unless it reached yad soledes bo, since there is no gravy there; and in Hagahot Maimoniyot at the end of chapter 5 of the laws of Pesach he wrote, and this is his language: a peel does not suffice except for something whose prohibition is noten ta'am, but chametz, which is b'mashahu, is forbidden even in roasting (see above seif 1); and so too Rabbenu Shabtai and Mahari of Strasbourg forbid even only through rinsing in a kli sheini — end of his words; and afterward he wrote that wheat found in water, even cold, the water is forbidden — end of his words; if so, they contradict each other, and one cannot say that in the first part it deals with [a case] without gravy, for he wrote rinsing in a kli rishon, and it is impossible to rinse in a kli rishon except in water; and one must say that in cold they forbid only the water, but if meat is soaked in it they do not forbid it, for cold lacks the power to absorb into it so much; but in hot everything is forbidden, and so it appears from his language that he wrote the water is forbidden; but if afterward they cooked a dish in that water, they certainly forbid the dish; but Rama, who wrote in siman 467 to forbid also the meat that remained in the water — if so, one must say as we said; and in Darkei Moshe siman 467 he wrote the law of cold that it is forbidden in the name of Mordechai, and afterward wrote in the name of Mordechai: if the chicken was salted in a chametz bowl, which is a kli sheini, it is forbidden, and only when it reached yad soledes bo — end of his words; and it is possible to divide that specifically when chametz is in actual presence they forbid in cold, but here, where it comes to discharge absorbed taste from the vessel, it does not forbid in cold; however, in Mordechai there it implies that from the taste of something poured he forbade it — see there; and so too the law in Hagahot Ashri — if so, there is no proof to forbid a kli sheini (see siman 451 seif 1); and furthermore, for he wrote in the name of Hagahot Maimoniyot chapter 1 that in hot, all the more so one need not be concerned, and one must say it is a different gloss; and per what was said above, therefore it appears to me that what Mordechai wrote to forbid the meat in cold is because there are scales in it, as written in Yoreh De'ah end of siman 91 and see siman 465 what he wrote; but with whole sides it is permitted — only the water is forbidden; and what he wrote in seif 5 to forbid fish soaked in a chametz vessel, etc., is to buy them l'chatchila: and it appears to me that if [liquid] spilled from a kli rishon onto something cold one need not be stringent at all, and all the more so one need not be stringent with leafy greens; but when they placed on it a piece of boiling meat in a bowl one should be stringent, for the poskim wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 94 that with such a thick item it is always like a kli rishon as long as it reached yad soledes bo, and see siman 318 seif 9 that there are things that cook in a kli rishon.
magen-avraham/8:א: With a new knife. But if the knife is old, even if it is not ben yomo it is forbidden, for it is sharp; and even before they were pickled — not like Shach and Avodat HaKodesh, who wrote specifically that they were cut after they were pickled, then they are sharp; for on the contrary Tur wrote that when one places water on them their sharpness is nullified, but rather it deals with [a case] before they were pickled, and so too the Tosafot; and nullification does not apply, for we measure against the entire knife; and if so, all the olives returned to chametz (Tur) — he explained that each one absorbed a bit from the knife, and if so each one became absorbed with chametz and did not discharge again; and even though it was ruled in Yoreh De'ah siman 106 that the prohibition returns and discharges — this applies in cooking, but in pickling it does not discharge, as was said regarding hag'alah, for we require specifically that it was cooked, as above; and the above section wrote that this law is according to one who says it returns and revives, and we do not hold thus, as written in seif 4 — and this is not so, for Tur wrote plainly that it does not return and revive, and afterward immediately the law of olives; therefore the words of Shach in Yoreh De'ah siman 96 are primary, and so too here Bach, and see Yoreh De'ah siman 111 in the words of the later authorities; and it appears to me that this is comparable to a piece of meat that fell into several pots one after another, which do not combine; but the brine of the olives is permitted for everyone, for the chametz is nullified in them in sixty; and even though we hold chanan, and if so we would require sixty against all the olives — nevertheless here, since before Pesach it is still permitted, we do not say chanan, as written in Yoreh De'ah siman 94 seif 6; and even per what was written in seif 5 that chametz, since its name was placed upon it, is not nat bar nat — nevertheless for this matter it has the law of permitted, that we do not say chanan, for many poskim do not say chanan in any prohibition except meat in milk: and if the olives were cooked before Pesach, even the olives themselves return to being permitted, for chametz returns and is discharged and the taste is nullified in sixty; and even though in Shulchan Aruch siman 106 it is written that that piece is forbidden — nevertheless behold Maharam Lublin wrote in his responsum: specifically where it absorbed a prohibition, but where it absorbed something permitted, even the piece itself is permitted, and so too Taz; however it appears to me that even though it is permitted to keep them, nevertheless it is forbidden to eat them on Pesach, for the plain meaning of Shulchan Aruch and the gloss in siman 106 implies the prohibition is not fully discharged from it; and if so, even though Taz and Maharam are lenient with meat — that is even if we say meat remained in it, all the more so we are not concerned; not so with chametz, which forbids in any amount; and furthermore, for otherwise some say it returns and revives, as written in seif 4.
